chapters.title: The Surprising Power of Atomic Habits
chapters.keys: Stop chasing goals and build systems: pick tiny habits and repeat them daily, because results are the compound interest of those habits. His term atomic habits means small routines that are both tiny and a source of great power. Get one percent better each day and in a year you are about 37 times better; get one percent worse and you sink toward zero. Expect the Plateau of Latent Potential, his name for the stretch where work piles up unseen before results break through, and do not quit in that valley of disappointment. Goals set direction, but winners and losers share the same goals, a reached goal changes you only for a moment, and putting happiness off until the goal is reached limits you, so the system is what makes progress. You do not rise to your goals; you fall to the level of your systems. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Dave Brailsford took over British Cycling, a team that had won little, and went after many small gains in everything from bike seats to riders' pillows to hand washing; about five years later the team took 60 percent of the road and track cycling gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, and British riders went on to win the Tour de France.

chapters.title: How Your Habits Shape Your Identity (and Vice Versa)
chapters.keys: Build identity-based habits, not outcome-based ones: decide who you want to be, then prove it to yourself with small wins. He names three layers of change, outcomes, then processes, then identity at the core, and says most people start at the wrong end. His two steps: first decide the type of person you want to be, then show it with small repeated actions. Every action is a vote for the type of person you are becoming, so you need a steady pile of votes, not a perfect record. Once a habit is part of who you are, you stop needing to push yourself to do it, and real change is identity change. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Brian Clark, an entrepreneur, had bitten his nails all his life; he began paying for manicures, and once his nails looked good he grew proud of them and stopped biting. He also tells of two people turning down a cigarette, one saying they are trying to quit and the other saying they are not a smoker; the second has changed who they are.

chapters.title: How to Build Better Habits in 4 Simple Steps
chapters.keys: Learn the four steps of every habit, in this order: cue, the trigger that predicts a reward; craving, the wanting that drives you; response, the action itself; reward, the payoff you were after. The cue and craving form the problem phase, and the response and reward form the solution phase. Habits are mental shortcuts learned from experience, and they free your mind for other things. From the four steps come his four laws of behavior change: make it obvious, make it attractive, make it easy, make it satisfying. To break a bad habit, invert them: make it invisible, unattractive, difficult, unsatisfying. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: psychologist Edward Thorndike put cats in puzzle boxes that opened when a lever was pressed; at first the cats scrambled about until they got out by chance, but over repeated trials they learned to do it almost at once, and he concluded that behavior followed by a satisfying result tends to be repeated.

chapters.title: The Man Who Didn't Look Right
chapters.keys: Before you change habits, see them: you cannot fix what you do not notice, because habits run on cues you have stopped seeing. His tool, the Habits Scorecard, is a list of your daily actions in order, each marked good, bad or neutral, judged by whether it moves you toward the person you want to be. His second tool, Pointing-and-Calling, means saying out loud the action you are about to take and what will follow, which forces awareness of an automatic act. The more automatic a behavior becomes, the less you notice it, so you must drag it into conscious view. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: a woman who had worked for years as a paramedic looked at her father-in-law at a family gathering and said he did not look right; she insisted he go to the hospital, where tests found a blocked major artery and he had surgery, because years of experience had trained her to spot the signs. Japanese train operators use Pointing-and-Calling, which cuts their errors sharply.

chapters.title: The Best Way to Start a New Habit
chapters.keys: Give every new habit a set time and place instead of waiting for inspiration. An implementation intention is a plan in the form I will do this behavior at this time in this location. Habit stacking is pairing the new habit with one you already do: after my current habit, I will do the new one. Clear says stacking works because one behavior tends to trigger the next. Choose a cue that fits, with the right frequency and timing, and make it specific. People who make a concrete plan for when and where are far more likely to follow through. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: British researchers split people into groups to build an exercise habit, and the group that wrote down when and where they would exercise did far better, with 91 percent exercising at least once a week. He also tells how the philosopher Denis Diderot, poor until he sold his library, got a fine scarlet robe; next to it his other belongings looked shabby, so he replaced them one after another.

chapters.title: Motivation Is Overrated; Environment Often Matters More
chapters.keys: Stop leaning on motivation and design your surroundings so the cue for a good habit is plain to see. Put the thing in sight: fruit in a bowl on the counter, the guitar in the middle of the room. Every habit starts with a cue, and vision is your strongest sense, so small changes in what you see change what you do. Habits get tied to a context, not just one trigger, so use one space for one use, and if you cannot get a new space, split the one you have by activity. A fresh environment makes new habits easier because old cues are not fighting you. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Anne Thorndike, a doctor at Massachusetts General Hospital, changed the hospital cafeteria by putting bottled water in the fridges by the registers and in baskets around the room, without saying a word; soda sales dropped and water sales rose by 25.8 percent over three months.

chapters.title: The Secret to Self-Control
chapters.keys: Do not try to win by willpower; cut the cue out of your life. The inversion of the first law is make it invisible: remove the trigger of a bad habit from your environment. People who seem to have great self-control simply spend less time in tempting situations. Once a habit is wired in, the urge comes back when the cue shows up, so resisting is a losing game and removing the cue is the winning one. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: during the Vietnam War many American soldiers used heroin, and some 20 percent became addicted; researcher Lee Robins found that after coming home only about 5 percent became re-addicted within a year, because they had left behind the environment full of cues.

chapters.title: How to Make a Habit Irresistible
chapters.keys: Make the good habit attractive by tying it to something you want. Dopamine rises when you anticipate a reward, not only when you get it, so the wanting is what moves you to act. Temptation bundling means you allow yourself something you want only while doing something you need to do. Combine it with habit stacking, which means tying a new habit to one you already do: after my current habit, I do the habit I need; after the habit I need, I do the habit I want. The more attractive an opportunity is, the more likely it is to become a habit. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Ronan Byrne, an engineering student, rigged his exercise bike to his laptop so that Netflix played only while he pedaled at a set speed, which tied his exercise to a show he wanted to watch.

chapters.title: The Role of Family and Friends in Shaping Your Habits
chapters.keys: Join a culture where your desired behavior is the normal behavior, and where you already have something in common with the group. We copy three groups: the close, meaning family and friends; the many, meaning the tribe; and the powerful, meaning those with status. The urge to belong is so strong that we follow the group even against our own judgment. When changing your habits means going against the tribe, change is hard; when it means fitting in, change is attractive. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Laszlo Polgar believed genius is made, raised his three daughters at home with chess at the center of their lives, and all three became chess prodigies, with Judit becoming a grandmaster younger than Bobby Fischer had.

chapters.title: How to Find and Fix the Causes of Your Bad Habits
chapters.keys: Find the deep motive behind a bad habit and reframe what the habit means to you. Every craving is the surface form of a deeper motive such as saving energy, getting food, winning approval or reducing uncertainty, and a habit is just your learned way to meet it. Reframe by saying you get to do a hard thing instead of you have to. A motivation ritual is something you enjoy that you do right before a hard habit, so the hard habit takes on the good feeling. The inversion: make the bad habit unattractive by listing the benefits of quitting it. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: in Istanbul, the author's guide Mike, who had quit smoking, said he quit because of Allen Carr's book on stopping smoking, which reframes what smoking gives you until cigarettes seem to offer nothing.

chapters.title: Walk Slowly, but Never Backward
chapters.keys: Start with repetitions, not with planning the perfect approach. He separates motion, planning and strategizing that feels like progress but produces nothing, from action, the behavior that produces a result. People stay in motion to put off the risk of failing. Habits form from the number of times you repeat a behavior, not from how much time passes; each repetition makes the behavior more automatic until it crosses what he calls the habit line, the point where you can do it with little thought. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Jerry Uelsmann, a photography professor at the University of Florida, split a class in two, grading one half on quantity and the other on the quality of one photo; the best photos came from the quantity group, who had taken many shots and learned from their mistakes.

chapters.title: The Law of Least Effort
chapters.keys: Make the good habit easy by cutting the friction between you and the action. The Law of Least Effort says people drift toward the option that takes the least work. Remove points of friction from good habits, an idea he calls addition by subtraction after Japanese manufacturers who cut wasted steps from production; and add friction to bad habits so they become harder to do. Prime the environment so it is ready for your next use, such as laying out what you need ahead of time. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Jared Diamond notes that Eurasia stretches east to west and the Americas north to south, so crops spread more easily across Eurasia where the climate stayed similar, and less friction meant faster spread.

chapters.title: How to Stop Procrastinating by Using the Two-Minute Rule
chapters.keys: Shrink any new habit to a version that takes under two minutes, then just start. The Two-Minute Rule says that when you start a new habit, it should take less than two minutes to do. Read one page instead of a book; put on running shoes instead of running a marathon. Decisive moments are small choices that set the course for the next hours, and a gateway habit is the easy first step that leads you onto the right path. Master the art of showing up first, because a habit must be established before it can be improved, then scale up step by step. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: one reader went to the gym every day but made a rule not to stay longer than five minutes; after a few weeks he began staying longer, and he went on to lose over 100 pounds. Choreographer Twyla Tharp starts each day by hailing a cab to the gym, and that one act sets off her whole routine.

chapters.title: How to Make Good Habits Inevitable and Bad Habits Impossible
chapters.keys: Lock in good behavior ahead of time so the good choice becomes the only one. A commitment device is a choice you make now that controls what you do later. Make onetime choices that keep paying off, like buying a good mattress or unsubscribing from emails. Automate with technology wherever you can so the behavior runs without you. The inversion: make bad habits impossible by raising the friction until you cannot act on the urge. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Victor Hugo had his assistant lock away his clothes so he could not go out, kept only a shawl, and wrote The Hunchback of Notre Dame, finishing early.

chapters.title: The Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change
chapters.keys: Add an immediate reward to good habits, because what is immediately rewarded gets repeated and what is immediately punished gets avoided, the Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change. Our brains grew in an immediate-return environment, but we now live in a delayed-return one, so good habits pay later and bad habits pay now. Make it satisfying by giving yourself an instant payoff for the right action. One use: open an account, and each time you skip a purchase, move that money into it. The immediate reward gets the habit going until identity takes over and keeps it going. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: public health worker Stephen Luby gave families in Karachi, Pakistan, a premium soap that lathered well and smelled good, and the pleasant experience made handwashing a habit, cutting diarrhea in children by 52 percent.

chapters.title: How to Stick with Good Habits Every Day
chapters.keys: Track your habits and never miss twice. A habit tracker is a simple record, such as a calendar where you cross off each day you do the habit. Tracking works three ways: it is obvious because it reminds you to act, attractive because you see progress, and satisfying because the record feels good. Never miss twice means one slip is fine but you get back on track at once. Reversal: Clear says tracking is not for everyone and warns that a measure can mislead once it becomes the goal, so you should not chase the number over what it is meant to show. Story the author tells: Trent Dyrsmid, a young stockbroker in Abbotsford, Canada, set two jars on his desk with 120 paper clips in one and moved a clip to the other with each sales call, keeping at it every day; his book of business grew fast.

chapters.title: How an Accountability Partner Can Change Everything
chapters.keys: Make a bad habit painful right away by putting someone else on watch. The inversion of the fourth law is make it unsatisfying: tie an instant cost to the bad behavior. A habit contract is an agreement that spells out your commitment and the penalty if you break it, signed by one or two people who hold you to it. An accountability partner is the person who watches and makes failure costly in front of others. Knowing someone is watching is a strong motivator, because we care what others think of us. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Bryan Harris, an entrepreneur in Nashville, signed a habit contract with his wife and his personal trainer committing to log his food and weigh himself; if he failed, he had to dress up for work and on Sunday mornings for the rest of the quarter, and each missed day of food logging cost him $200 paid to his trainer. He later raised the stakes with cash penalties to his trainer and his wife, and he lost the weight.

chapters.title: The Truth About Talent (When Genes Matter and When They Don't)
chapters.keys: Choose habits and fields that fit your natural abilities, so the odds are on your side. Genes do not decide your destiny; they decide where you have the best chance. Explore widely first, then exploit what works: ask what feels like fun to you and like work to others, what makes you lose track of time, and where you get better results than average. If you cannot win by being better, win by being different, carving out a niche where you stand out. Reversal: Clear says genes do not remove the need for hard work, but hard work in a field that does not suit your genes will not get you as far, so choose your field with care. Story the author tells: swimmer Michael Phelps and runner Hicham El Guerrouj differ in height by several inches but wore the same pants length, because Phelps has a long torso and short legs that suit swimming, and El Guerrouj long legs that suit running.

chapters.title: The Goldilocks Rule: How to Stay Motivated in Life and Work
chapters.keys: Work on tasks at the edge of your current ability to stay motivated. The Goldilocks Rule says people are most motivated when a task is neither too hard nor too easy, but just manageable. When a task is too easy you get bored; too hard and you get discouraged. Flow comes when the challenge sits a bit past what you can already do. The greatest threat to success is not failure but boredom, so learn to fall in love with doing the same work again and again. Professionals stick to the schedule even when it feels dull; amateurs let the mood decide. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Steve Martin got a job at Disneyland at age ten, selling guidebooks and then working in the park's magic shop. Over years of performing he grew his act by only a minute or two each year, keeping the jokes that worked, until he became one of the most successful comedians of his day.

chapters.title: The Downside of Creating Good Habits
chapters.keys: Pair habits with deliberate practice and regular review, because a habit on autopilot stops getting better. Once a habit is automatic you stop noticing small errors, so habits alone stop making you better and you need to add deliberate practice and review. Mastery is habits plus deliberate practice: once one skill is automatic, push on to the next. Reflection and review means checking how you are doing on a set schedule; Clear writes an Annual Review of his habits and progress and an Integrity Report on whether he is living by his values. Keep your identity loose, so that losing one role does not break you. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: after the Los Angeles Lakers lost in the 1986 playoffs, coach Pat Riley gave his players a program called Career Best Effort, tracking each player's stats against a baseline and asking each to improve by at least 1 percent over the season. The Lakers won the championship about eight months later, in that same season, and won again the following year.
